div.head: Objective
div.p: Individuals affected by psychosis often have deficits in several neurocognitive functions. Prospective Memory (PM), the ability to remember to do things, is crucial for activities of daily living, social and occupational functioning, but very few studies have attempted to examine this domain of functioning in people with psychosis, particularly in India. Methods 71 patients with psychosis, (both early and established psychosis), and 140 age, gender, and education matched healthy controls (HC) were assessed using the Positive Negative Symptom Scale (PANSS), Hospital Anxiety and Depression scale (HADS), and Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination (ACE-III). PM was assessed using the Cambridge Prospective Memory Test (CAMPROMT) and the Prospective and Retrospective Memory Questionnaire (PRMQ). Group differences were evaluated using Mann-Whitney U Tests.

div.head: Results
div.p: Significantly greater cognitive deficits, higher anxiety, and depression were evident in the psychosis group when compared with controls. The psychosis group performed significantly poorer on both timeand event-based tests in CAMPROMPT than controls. These differences remained when controlling for age, education, general cognitive functioning and mood. The subjective measure of PM (PRMQ) did not differentiate the two groups. The PM performance of early and established psychosis patients was similar. Comparisons with cross cultural data (PMRQ UK norms and CAMPROMPT & PMRQ Chinese study) revealed important differences in PM performance.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Individuals with psychosis have significant deficits in both time-and event-based PM. CAMPROMPT emerged as a more sensitive PM measure in comparison with PRMQ, which only identified RM deficits in the clinical sample. RM difficulties were more commonly reported by the established psychosis group compared to the early psychosis group, suggesting differences in the level of problem awareness or adaptation strategies. Results of the cross cultural comparisons of the study data underscores the need for cultural contextualization of assessments.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Chronic disorders, such as schizophrenia and psychotic bipolar disorders, are amongst the most serious and enduring mental health disorders. A recent study by the India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative Mental Disorders Collaborators in 2020 reported a prevalence of 0.3% (95% CI, 0.2-0.3) for schizophrenia, noting that prevalence has increased since 1990.

Schizophrenia imposes significant socio-economic burden on affected individuals, their families, and wider society (Vasudeva, Shekar, & Rao, 2013;Chavan, Das, Garg, Puri & Banavaram, 2018). Research on neuropsychological functioning associated with these disorders has identified evidence of a wide range of deficits in cognitive functioning, including in the domains of executive and social cognition (Quiles, Prouteau & Verdoux 2013;Bliksted, Fagerlund, Weed, Frith & Videbech. 2014). It has been reported that individuals in the early and chronic stages of psychosis and, also those at risk of developing psychosis, have deficits in working memory, verbal memory, executive function, and sensory gating that are mediated by complex neuroanatomical and neurophysiological substrates (Kim et al. 2003;Canuet et al. 2010;Zhao et al. 2011;Dutt et al. 2015;Shaikh et al. 2015).

The question of whether people with psychosis show abnormal deterioration in cognitive functioning over time has proved to be controversial, with studies and reviews drawing different conclusions. For example, Bora and Murray's (2014) review concluded that patients with first episode psychosis and people at ultra-high risk of psychosis show no evidence of decline, and in fact improve, in verbal working memory and executive functioning over time.

Similarly, Barder et al. (2013) reported a 10 year follow up of neurocognitive functions in people with first episode psychosis and concluded that there was long-term stability, with the exception of verbal memory in patients with psychotic relapse. However, other recent studies have found that people with a diagnosis of schizophrenia or other psychoses showed decline in IQ, verbal knowledge and memory, but not processing speed or executive function (Zanelli et al., 2019), leading some to conclude that "the cognitive decline that begins years or even decades before the onset of the first psychosis continues for many years afterwards" (Khan, 2019, p775). The presence of multiple confounders, including the effects of the illness itself and/or the use of long-term psychotropics, potentially makes the clinical picture more complex. Yet, what seems to be evident is that most patients have markedly poor outcomes, with significant cognitive changes affecting their social and occupational functioning, often requiring long term rehabilitation in secondary and tertiary psychiatric services (Nuechterlein, 2019;Silverstein & Wilkniss, 2004;Barlati et. al. 2013).

An aspect of cognition that has been relatively under-researched in psychosis is prospective memory (Shum, Leung, Ungvari & Tang, 2001), although interest has increased lately because of its relevance to real-world everyday activities. Prospective memory (PM) is the ability to perform previously planned actions at a particular time in the future (time-based prospective memory) (TBPM) or when an event occurs (event-based prospective memory) (EBPM). For example, remembering to attend a doctor's consultation, taking medications on time, or passing on a message to a family member, which can be integral to the long-term wellbeing of patients with psychosis and are considered daily living tasks, are important examples of prospective memory tasks. Einstein & McDaniel (2005), in their multiple process model of prospective memory, stated that successful completion of a prospective memory task requires encoding of an intention, retention of the intended action, and monitoring for the environmental event associated with the task and that the presence of a target cue is expected to spontaneously initiate the retrieval of prospective memory. This suggests the involvement of attention, monitoring, and long-term memory in the successful completion of prospective memory tasks.

In a meta-analysis of 29 case-control studies, Zhou et al. (2019) reported that patients with schizophrenia were significantly poorer than healthy controls on tests of time-based, event-based and activity-based prospective memory. In addition, they concluded that there were significant differences between older and younger patients (older worse), lower and higher education (lower worse) and between chronic and first-episode patients (chronic worse).

Impaired PM is also one of the major causes of poor compliance with medication regimens (Zogg et al., 2012), something that affects 50% of patients with schizophrenia (Bebbington et al., 1995). Even though impairment in PM significantly affects independent living (Fleming et al. 2008) it is rarely examined in the standard neuropsychological assessment of patients with schizophrenia or other neuropsychiatric conditions. The few tests and questionnaires available to measure prospective memory have been developed and standardized in the West.

Questionnaires for measuring PM by self-report or informants include the Prospective Memory Questionnaire (PMQ) (Hannon, Adams, Harrington, Fries-Dias & Gipson, 1995) the Prospective and Retrospective memory questionnaire (PRMQ) (Crawford, Smith, Maylor, Della Sala & Logie, 2003;Smith, Della Sala, Logie & Maylor, 2000) and the Comprehensive Assessment of Prospective Memory (CAPM) (Chau, Lee, Fleming, Roche & Shum 2007).

Objective performance tests to assess PM include the Memory for Intentions test (Raskin et al. 2004), the Modified Six Elements test, a subtest of the Behavioural Assessment of the Dysexecutive Syndrome (Wilson et al. 1996) and the Cambridge Prospective Memory Test (CAMPROMPT) (Wilson et al. 2005). The CAMPROMPT has a test-retest reliability of 0.64 and satisfactory convergent and construct validity (Wilson et al. 2005). It is designed to assess both TBPM and EBPM to simulate routine daily tasks.

The role of culture and how it influences cognitive performance is currently a topic of active debate (Fernandez & Abe, 2018). Studies have demonstrated that culture-specific attitudes can influence performance on timed neuropsychological tests (Ardilla, 1995;Agranovich, 2007). Cross-cultural differences in prospective memory have been reported in a study comparing Chinese and Canadian adults (Chang, 2013). Previous research has also shown cultural effects on epidemiology, phenomenology, outcome, and treatment of mental illness , especially in schizophrenia and affective disorders (Viswanath & Chaturvedi 2012;Sartorius N et al., 1986). Prospective memory deficits in schizophrenia have been studied mainly using experimental paradigms in western populations (Zhou et al. 2012;Au et al. 2014;Zhou et al. 2014;Khoyratty et al. 2015;Man et al. 2016;Zhou et al. 2017;Lin, 2019). None of these studies have used a standardized measure for the assessment of prospective memory or examined patients with early psychosis.

The present study therefore, aimed to: (a) compare the performance of patients with psychosis and healthy controls on a standardized test of prospective memory As it has been noted that symptoms of psychosis, particularly negative symptoms, may be associated with cognitive performance (e.g. Peng et al., 2021) the association between symptoms and CAMPROMPT performance was examined. In addition, we explored whether prospective memory performance would be explained by impairment in general cognition reflected by performance on a cognitive screening tool (Addenbrookes Cognitive Examination III). This was important because if PM performance is strongly predicted by performance on a brief cognitive screen then in clinical practice it may not be necessary to specifically assess PM. Mood disorder is associated with poorer cognitive performance (Snyder, 2013) and is a common co-occurring condition in people with schizophrenia (Upthegrove et al., 2017), hence this makes it necessary to evaluate the association between mood and PM performance. Examination of these factors also allowed us to examine whether any differences between patients with psychosis and healthy controls remained when after controlling for any significant symptom, general cognitive or mood factors. The study results could help to develop strong recommendations for a culturally appropriate indices that may be used as objective markers in early intervention strategies and rehabilitation programs for patients with schizophrenia in India.

div.head: Sample/Participants
div.p: Our sample comprised 140 healthy controls (HC) and 71 individuals diagnosed with psychotic disorders (PSx). Patients with psychosis accessing the outpatient and in-patient services in Duttanagar Mental Health Centre, Kolkata, India were invited to participate in the study. The patient group included those with early psychosis (illness duration ≤ 3 years from time of first symptom) and with established psychosis (illness duration >3 years from time of first symptom). The psychosis group included patients with schizophrenia (n = 45), schizoaffective disorders (n = 20), psychotic bipolar (n = 6) disorders. Power analysis suggests that this sample size was adequate to provide 80% power to detect an effect size as low as d=0.41 (r 2 =0.04) and provides 99% power to detect an effect size of d=0.78 (r 2 =0.13), which was observed in the study of Raskin et al. (2014).

The healthy cohort comprised both males and females between the ages of 18 and 65 years, with a minimum of five years of education, such that they were able to understand the instructions of the study. Those with a documented medical history of neurological disorders (e.g., stroke, epilepsy, traumatic head injury, multiple sclerosis, movement disorder, and brain tumor), alcohol/substance abuse known to affect the function of the central nervous system for the past year were excluded. They were recruited from outpatient and community settings in Kolkata and Bangalore, two major cosmopolitan centers in India.

div.head: Questionnaires and Cognitive Screening
div.p: Demographic data were collected including gender, age, language, ethnicity, education, occupation, and medication history. Data for illness duration and age of onset of illness was collected for the patient group along with the history of psychotropics. The severity of symptoms associated with schizophrenia was measured using the Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale (PANSS) (Kay et al. 1987). For assessment of mood and anxiety, the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) (Zigmond and Snaith 1983) The tool has been translated and adapted in numerous Indian languages. In the current study Bengali, Hindi, and Indian English versions were used.

div.head: Prospective Memory Assessment
div.p: Prospective memory was evaluated with the Prospective and Retrospective Memory Questionnaire-PMRQ (Smith et al. 2000) and the Cambridge Prospective Memory Test -CAMPROPMT (Wilson et al. 2005). The PRMQ consists of 16 questions rated on a fivepoint Likert scale by the patient and an informant separately. In our study, we used only the self-rating version of the scale. CAMPROMPT (Wilson et al. 2005) comprises four timebased and four event-based prospective memory tasks. Participants are required to remember to carry out intentions after a specific time duration or the occurrence of an event, as they continue to be occupied with intellectually demanding filler tasks. They can observe the time using a clock and use strategies such as note keeping to help them remember intentions. The administration of the CAMPROMT test was slightly modified by incorporating tests from the neuropsychological battery such as Digit Span and the Brixton Spatial Anticipation Test instead of the standard quiz as described in the manual. These tests are not reported in the current study. Event-based and Time-based scores are reported.

The HADS, PRMQ, and instructions of CAMPROMPT were translated into Hindi and Bengali by a language expert along with a neuropsychologist. The translated questionnaires were back-translated subsequently by two subject experts (a psychiatrist and a neuropsychologist) to confirm the accuracy of the translation. CAMPROMPT has been previously translated, modified for the Chinese speaking adults by Man et al. (2016), and has also been validated for Chinese patients with psychosis.

div.head: Procedure
div.p: Individuals who agreed to participate in the study were briefed about the procedures. All participants were then administered the following scales -PANSS, HADS & ACE-III followed by the CAMPROMPT and PRMQ. All demographic, clinical, and neuropsychological data were tabulated in Microsoft Excel and reviewed for completeness and errors. Data analysis was conducted using IBM-SPSS version 20.

div.head: Data Analysis
div.p: All variables were examined for outliers and tested for normality. For data that could not be normalized with standard transformations, non-parametric tests were used. Group differences between controls and patients in socio-demographic variables (age, gender, education) and clinical measures (PANSS, HADS, ACE-III, and PM Tests) were evaluated using inferential statistics such as Mann-Whitney U test and Chi-Squared as appropriate. Effect sizes were computed and reported as a correlation effect size (r). Similarly, the groups were compared on the CAMPROMPT and PRMQ using Mann-Whitney U tests.

Subsequently correlation analysis was conducted to examine if demographic (age, education, gender), symptom (PANSS), general cognition (ACE III) and mood (HADS) variables were correlated with CAMPROMPT Event and Time performance in the patient group. Similarly, in the control group correlation between demographic (age, education, gender), general cognition (ACE III) and mood (HADS) variables and CAMPROMPT Event and Time performance was assessed. All PM performance correlated variables for both patients or controls were then included in a multiple regression model, along with the Group variable (patients vs controls) to identify a parsimonious set of predictors that were significantly associated with CAMPROMPT performance.

Further, a sub-group analysis was conducted in three steps: a) Early Psychosis Vs Controls; b) Controls Vs Chronic Psychosis; c) Early Psychosis Vs Established Psychosis to determine if there were any prospective memory differences separately for the early and established psychosis patient groups.
The correlation between the objective measure of PM (CAMPROMPT) and the subjective measure of everyday memory difficulties (PRMQ) was examined with Spearman correlation.

div.head: Cross-cultural comparisons
div.p: A supplementary analysis was also conducted to compare data from our patient and healthy control samples on the CAMPROMPT and PRMQ with data from another published set of patient and healthy control samples from Asia (China) (Au, Xiang, Ungvari, Lee, Shum, Man, et. al. 2016). Since mean (SD) data were available for the Chinese data we conducted a one sample t-test to compare our data. We also compared our patient and healthy control data on the PRMQ with the original UK data (reference to be included).

div.head: Results
div.p: The study cohort comprised 140 healthy controls and 71 patients with psychosis. Of the 71 patients (schizophrenia (n-45), schizoaffective disorders (n-20), psychotic bipolar (n-6) disorders), 30 had early psychosis and the remaining 41 patients had established psychosis.

A descriptive summary of the demographics is presented in Table 1. The mean age of the healthy controls and patients was 33.56 (12.76) and 33.52 (11.76) years respectively and the mean formal education was 13.93(2.93) and 14.03 (3.03) years respectively.

div.head: Clinical Scales & Prospective Memory Test
div.p: In comparison to the healthy controls the patients had significantly higher scores on HADS-D, HADS-A and lower scores on ACE-III when compared with the controls (Table 2). Also, in keeping with expectations, patients were symptomatically different from controls in relation to positive and negative psychotic features but the groups were comparable on the PANSS general psychopathology scale. It is noteworthy that whilst the PANSS scores differed between the groups, the scores for the patients were nevertheless relatively low, reflecting the fact that patients were not experiencing severe acute psychosis symptoms at the time of participating in the study.
Comparisons on the PM test performances revealed that the patients performed significantly poorer on the objective PM tasks when compared with healthy adults, with large effect sizes.

div.head: Regression Analysis
div.p: In the patient group there was a significant correlation between CAMPROMPT Event and HADS-D (rho=-0.244, p=0.04), and between CAMPROMPT Time and age (rho=-0.257, p=0.03) and ACE III (rho=0.421, p<0.001). For healthy controls there were significant correlations between CAMPROMPT Event and ACE III (rho=0.192,p=0.02) and between CAMPROMPT Time and ACE III (rho=-0.244, p<0.001).

Multiple linear regression was used to examine how Group (patients and controls), age, HADS-D, and ACE-III predicted CAMPROMPT-Event and Time-based scores (Tables 4 and5). Our data met all assumptions of linear regression and for CAMPROMPT-Event the regression model was significant (F (4) = 40.811) with an R 2 = .44 & R 2 adjusted= .43 (See Table 3). The analysis shows that CAMPROMPT-Event was significantly and independently predicted by group, age, ACE-III and HADS-D. The histogram of standardized residuals indicated that the data contained approximately normally distributed errors, as did the normal P-P plot of standardized residuals. An analysis of standardized residuals was carried out, which showed that the data contained no outliers (Std. Residual Min= -3.18 Std Residual Max=2.45). Relevant tests for the assumption of collinearity indicated that multicollinearity was not a concern.

div.head: (TABLE 3)
div.p: For CAMPROMPT-Time, the regression model was also significant (F (4) = 66.504, p=<0.001) with R 2 = .57 & R 2 adjusted= 0.56 indicating that these variables explain a significant amount of variance in CAMPROMPT Time scores (See Table 4). The analysis shows that CAMPROMPT-Time was significantly and independently predicted by only group and ACE-III scores. The histogram of standardized residuals indicated that the data contained approximately normally distributed errors, as did the normal P-P plot of standardized residuals. An analysis of standard residuals was carried out, which showed that the data contained no outliers (Std. Residual Min= -3.10 Std Residual Max=2.93). Tests for examining the assumption of collinearity indicated that multicollinearity was not a concern.

div.head: Association between CAMPROMPT and PRMQ in patients with psychosis
div.p: We found that CAMPROMPT Event scores had a significant correlation with PRMQ-R (rho=-0.40, p<0.05). However, there were no significant correlations between CAMPROMPT Event scores and PRMQ-P (rho=-0.29), CAMPROMPT-Time and PRMQ-R (rho=-0.25) and CAMPROMPT-Time and PRMQ-P (rho=-.026).

div.head: Comparison between our Indian participants with participants from China on the CAMPROMPT
div.p: A comparison of our study data to the data from a Chinese healthy cohort and patients with schizophrenia (Au, Xiang, Ungvari, Lee, Shum, Man, et. al. 2016) was conducted. Our patient group had a lower performance on the CAMPROMPT Time (Chinese mean = 11.1, Indian mean=9.62, t=-3.03, p=.003), but were not different on CAMPROMPT Event (Chinese mean = 12.1, Indian mean=11.82, t=-.59, p=.557). The Indian healthy controls performed significantly better than the Chinese healthy individuals for CAMPROMPT Time (Chinese mean = 14.6, Indian mean=15.9, t=5.50, p<.001) and for CAMPROMPT Event (Chinese mean = 14.9, Indian mean=16.4, t=8.60, p<.001).

div.head: Comparison between our Indian participants with original UK PRMQ data
div.p: The PRMQ data from the current study was compared with the original Crawford norms for the scale (Crawford, Henry, Ward & Blake, 2006). We found that our healthy adults scored significantly lower than the normative UK sample on PRMQ-P (UK Mean = 20.18 (4.91); Indian Mean = 15.86 (5.98) ; t =8.87, p <0.01) and PRMQ-R (UK Mean = 18.69 (4.98); Indian Mean = 14.23 (4.83) ; t=9.52, p-<0.01). Our patients also scored significantly lower than the normative UK sample on PRMQ-P (t= 4.51, p-<0.01) and PRMQ-R (t= 4.05, p-<0.01).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: In the present study, we examined prospective memory performance in Indian patients with psychosis using a standardized test measure (the CAMPROMPT) in a cultural context not previously examined. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first Indian study that has specifically examined prospective memory deficits in both early psychosis and established psychosis along with controls, in a cosmopolitan population.

The CAMPROMPT has never been formally used to assess Prospective Memory in the Indian subcontinent. We found that the translated and modified CAMPROMPT was easy to comprehend for the participants, including individuals with low education who were able to engage with the task instructions.

Despite comparable age, education, and gender, patients performed significantly worse on the CAMPROMPT when compared with healthy controls. Patient performance was consistently poor in both time and event-based PM tasks. Our findings are congruent with previous studies which reported PM deficits in patients with psychosis (Elvevag, Maylor & Gilbert 2003;Shum. et al., 2004;Kumar, Nizame & Jahan 2005;Henry, Rendell, Kliegel & Altgassen 2007;Altgassen, Kliegel, Rendell, Henry & Zollig 2008;Chan, Shum, Toulopoulou & Chen 2008;Ungvari, Xiang, Tang & Shum 2008;Wang. et al. 2009). A possible explanation of PM deficits in patients with psychosis can be attributed to the overall cognitive impairments found in these patients (Mohamed, Paulsen, O'Leary Arnd & Andreasen 1999;Kuperberg & Heckers 2000;Townsend, Malla & Norman 2001;Sheffield, Karcher, Barch & Sciences 2019;Bowie & Harvey 2006). However, there were differences between the patient group and the controls even when taking into account the general cognitive difficulties reflected in ACE III scores, suggesting that deficits other than those reflected in the ACE III may be contributing to impaired PM performance. PM tasks rely heavily on intact functioning of cognitive abilities such as attention, memory, planning, and self-monitoring (Martin, Brown & Hicks 2011, Gonneaud & Kalpouzos 2011) and some of these constructs are not assessed by the ACE III. A reduced ability to either remember, maintain, monitor, or shift from the ongoing task and retrieve intentions when required might lead to poor performance of these individuals on an objective measure of PM.

In the subgroup analysis, age and education matched controls were compared to patients with early and established psychosis groups separately. Both groups were impaired when compared with controls. Our findings are corroborated by Lui et al., (2011), Altgassen. et al., (2008); Chan. et al. (2008); Wang. et al. (2009);and Ungvari. et al. (2008). Given the presence of executive dysfunction in these patients which is closely associated with PM, deficits in PM are as predicted. There has been increasing functional neuroimaging and electrophysiological evidence that shows altered activation of the prefrontal cortex in patients with early psychosis in comparison to healthy subjects (Winterer et al. 2000;Mulert et al. 2001;Gallinat et al. 2002;Dutt et al. 2015;Martínez-Cengotitabengoa et al. 2014). Also, previous research has indicated the presence of these cognitive deficits in these patients at an early stage (Niendam et al. 2006;Chang. et al. 2013;Leeson et al. 2009). Our findings of PM deficits in these patients are consistent with these previous findings.

Previous researchers such as Zanelli et al. (2019) have suggested that cognitive performance on tasks of IQ, Verbal knowledge and memory worsens over time. Our study, however, found the performance of both the patient sub-groups was comparable on the PM tasks. The comparable performance between groups, with very small effect sizes, found in our study, indicate that the PM deficit occurs in the initial stages of the illness and maintains throughout the illness progression (Chan et al. 2013), though this cannot be concluded definitively from this cross-sectional study that compared the groups at two stages of illness.

div.head: CAMPROMPT, symptoms of psychosis, overall cognitive function and mood
div.p: Neither positive nor negative symptoms were associated with CAMPROMPT Event or Time performance in our patient group. This contrasts with findings from Zhou. et al. (2012), who reported moderate correlations between PANSS N and both time and event based PM, although no correlation with PANSS P. The average PANSS score for our patient sample was relatively low, reflecting the fact that most patients were not experiencing severe symptoms of psychosis at the time of participating, which may account for the lack of evidence of a significant association with PM performance. ACE III performance was univariately associated with both CAMPROMPT Event and Time and was as an independent predictor in both regression models. Given that ACE III performance reflects a wide range of cognitive functions it is not surprising that it predicts PM performance, but it is interesting that the group (patient vs controls) variable was also an independent predictor of PM performance. This suggests that some other factor was influencing PM performance over and above general cognition. It may be that aspects of attention and executive functions not well captured by the ACE III, but implicated in PM process deficits, are responsible for this finding. Anxiety (HADS A) was not associated with PM performance, but depression was associated with CAMPROMPT Event (but not Time) and remained in the regression model as an independent predictor. Previous studies such as Arnold, Bayen & Bohm (2014), Rude, Hertel, Jarrold &Hedlbund (2010), andAlbinskini. Kliegel, Sedek &Kleszczewska-Albińska (2012) have reported an association between PM performance and depression. The lack of a significant association between anxiety and PM performance is contradictory to the findings of Bowman et al. (2019) who reported that anxiety rather than depression was associated with poor prospective memory, though this was in college students and not clinical populations.

Cognitive impairments in planning and monitoring have been consistently reported in patients with depression and anxiety. PM tasks require self-monitoring (Einstein and McDonald 2005) which seems to be affected in patients with depression (Bastiaansen et al. 2018;Twomey & O'Reilly 2018). Furthermore, cognitive deficits in patients with depression (Bremner et al., 2002;Menzies et al., 2007) are linked with prefrontal regions of the brain which are also implicated in PM tasks (Burgess, Quayle, Frith, 2001;Burgess et al.2008;Costa et al. 2011;Simons, Scholvnick, Gilbert, Frith & Burgess 2006). However, depression does not fully account for the difference between patients and controls in our study as there was a difference between the groups even when controlling for depression.

div.head: Subjective Vs Objective Measures of PM
div.p: The PRMQ-P and PRMQ-R had moderate correlations with CAMPROMPT event scores, though only the PRMQ-R was significant. Chan et al. (2008) in their study found no correlation between PRMQ and computer-based tasks. The association between PRMQ and CAMPROMPT event scores indicates the performance on CAMPROMPT might be associated with everyday difficulties faced by individuals. However, the correlations in our study were weak indicating the possibility of a wide range of factors including biological, psychological, sociocultural & environmental (Roper 2002) impacting everyday activities.

Interestingly in the current study, subjective measures assessing PM did not differentiate between the controls and patient groups. These findings are contradictory to previous research such as Bigdeli, Farzin &Talepasand (2014) andKim Jeong-Youn. et al. (2019) who reported significant differences in PRMQ performance in patients with first episode psychosis and schizophrenia when compared to controls. One of the reasons for such findings may be a lack of awareness in patients of their illness and symptoms (Amador, Strauss, Yale & Gorman 1991;David 1990). Owing to lack of insight, patients with psychosis may provide a poor estimation of their cognitive abilities. Uttl & Kibreab (2011) reported that self-report measures of prospective memory have good reliability but poor validity and should not be interpreted as reflecting PM ability. Another possible explanation of our findings is that the questions on the PMRQ rely on the successful completion of a prospective memory task, but do not focus on the steps involved in the completion of these tasks. For example, one question in the PRMQ is 'Do you forget to buy an item from a shop e.g., a birthday card, even when you see the shop?'. An individual might answer that they rarely forget but in reality, s/he could have had reminders to complete the task. Except for one question which mentions with no help from others or a diary, the remaining five PM questions in the PRMQ do not refer to remembering independently. Related to this latter point it was striking that both our healthy controls, and our patients, scored below the levels of the UK PRMQ normative data. Discussion with participants after the assessment revealed that patients often complete tasks as their family members tend to remind them, intricacies that are not tapped in the questionnaire. India being a collectivistic society (Jha & Singh 2011) shows more interdependence and co-operation (Chadha & Deb 2013) which provides good social support to the patient, so limiting everyday PM difficulties by scaffolding everyday PM performance, even though they would be present if the patients were required to rely on remembering themselves. If so, then people will not have the experience of making prospective memory errors as frequently as those in individualistic cultures where less scaffolding may be in place. Thus, it may be possible to detect cognitive impairments (i.e. with a test such as the CAMPROMPT) that would lead to everyday prospective memory difficulties if support for impaired cognition were not in place, but the presence of support for functioning may mean that everyday difficulties (measured on the PRMQ) do not occur as expected.

A multinational study conducted by the WHO (1979) reported a better prognosis in patients with schizophrenia in developing countries like India. These findings also support our findings of lesser problems in daily functioning in patients with psychosis. Further investigation of this would be useful.

The finding that our patients were similar to a Chinese sample on CAMPROMPT Event, but poorer on CAMPROMT Time, whilst our healthy controls had higher scores on both Event and Time tests than the Chinese sample, highlights that test performance in different cultural/linguistic contexts cannot be assumed to be similar. In relation to the healthy groups, our participants were older and less well educated than the Chinese sample, so it seems unlikely that these factors account for better performance in our sample. CAMPROMPT allows the use of notes/strategies for remembering (which is allowed in the CAMPROMPT) and this may have been different between our sample and the Chinese sample, however this aspect of performance could not be compared with the Chinese sample.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: Potential limitations of the study include the possible effects of psychotropic medications which were not examined in the current study. The use of non-parametric tests may have reduced the sensitivity of the data analysis, though significant differences between groups emerged as a result of sample and effect sizes. As noted, the average PANSS score for the patients was relatively low, reflecting the fact that most patients were not experiencing severe symptoms of psychosis at the time of participating. This limits the generalizability of our results to the more severely ill patients. Other limitations include the lack of more culturally specific measurement tools to capture PM in the South Asian setting. Both the subjective and objective tests used, were not developed in a South Asian setting and hence may have been influenced by cultural factors in present context, which were not present in the context where the tests were originally developed. To overcome potential limitations to answer wider questions and enhance the generalization of findings, a wide range of confounding factors have been identified and have been recommended to as inclusions in future studies, as noted.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In conclusion, this study demonstrates that PM deficits are prominent in patients with psychosis irrespective of their stage of illness. PM deficits are already present in the patients in the early phase of illness and continue to be evident as the disease progresses. PM deficits are also associated with mood indicating not only the complex nature of the illness but possible interactions in the association between psychosis and PM. This should be the focus of study for future research. Finally, these findings also highlight the importance of studying cognitive functions in the early stages of psychosis so that rehabilitation can be supported based on their cognitive deficits and strengths. Rehabilitation strategies focusing on PM deficits in these patients will aid them in dealing with poor compliance to medication (Zogg et al., 2012), which are noted in 50% of schizophrenic patients (Bebbington et al., 1995).

div.head: Comparison between Healthy Controls and Early Psychosis
div.p: The 31 early psychosis patients were matched on a 1:2 basis with a set of 62 controls, with matching based on age (p=0.86), education (p=0.92), and gender (p=0.37).

The comparison of PM performance of early psychosis group and matched controls, showed a similar pattern as seen in the comparison done with the whole group (Supplementary table 1). The patient group was significantly worse on the PM objective tasks as seen from their performance on CAMPROMPT-Time and Event. They were comparable to controls on the PRMQ.

div.head: Comparison between Healthy Controls and Patients with Established Psychosis
div.p: The 40 established psychosis patients were also matched on a 1:2 basis with a set of 80 controls, with matching based on age (p=0.46), education (p=0.33), and gender (p=0.95).

The comparison of PM performance of patients with established psychosis and matched controls showed a significantly worse performance in patients on the PM objective tasks -CAMPROMPT-time & event and the RM subset of PRMQ.

div.head: Comparison between patients with Established Psychosis and Early Psychosis
div.p: Both the groups were comparable on education (p=0.73) and gender (p=0.98). The patients with early psychosis were, as expected, significantly younger (p=<0.001) than the established psychosis group. The mean age of the early psychosis group was 34.71(12.14) and the mean age of patients with established psychosis was 36.15 (11.57). Interestingly the performance of both the groups was comparable on the prospective memory tasks across both objective and subjective measures of prospective memory as seen on CAMPROMPT Event, Time, PRMQ-P, and PRMQ-R (Supplementary table 3).
